content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a simple yet effective method AGgregatoR of dEtectors' dEcisions (AGREE) to aggregate the decisions based on the soft-probability outputs of multiple trained detectors. It evaluates the defense framework by tackling the problem of simultaneous adversarial examples detection. It validates AGREE on CIFAR10 and SVHN and shows that it consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art when simultaneous adversarial attacks are present at evaluation time.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
I think this paper has the following strengths:

1. It gives theoretical justification for the proposed method AGREE: it formalizes the simultaneous attacks detection setup as a minimax cross-entropy risk and derives a surrogate loss from which it formally characterizes the optimal soft-detector leading to AGREE. 

2. The writing is clear in general and the related works are properly discussed. 

However, I think this paper has the following weaknesses: 

1. The biggest concern is that it doesn't evaluate the proposed defense AGREE under strong enough adaptive attacks. Evaluating the defense under strong adaptive attacks is very important and the results under the adaptive attacks should be presented in the main paper. The adaptive attacks should have full knowledge of the defense mechanisms. In terms of AGREE, the adaptive attacks should know the model parameters of all the detectors used and know the weights $\\{ w^*_k \\}$ used to build the final detector in equation (10). The adaptive attack objective should be searching adversarial examples such that the final detector (equation (10)) fails to detect them as adversarial examples and the classifier gives wrong predictions on them. I don't think it evaluates AGREE under such adaptive attacks. It is very easy to come up with defenses that are robust against non-adaptive attacks. But those defenses usually have limited robustness under strong adaptive attacks (see [1]). So I think evaluating strong adaptive attacks is very important for demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed defense.  Besides, it should evaluate the proposed defense AGREE under the attacks proposed in [2], which are designed for adversarial example detection defenses. 

2. It doesn't include enough baselines for comparison in the experiments. I think it should compare the proposed defense method to [3][4], etc.

3. It doesn't perform ablation studies to validate each component of AGREE. In particular, it doesn't perform experiments to show if AGREE works for different kinds of detectors. In the experiments, it only shows the base where AGREE aggregates four simple pre-trained detectors. I think it should perform an ablation study on the number of detectors aggregated and different kinds of detectors. It claims that AGREE can aggregate existing detectors (possibly provided by a third party), but the experimental results don't demonstrate this. It is unclear if aggregating several existing adversarial example detectors using AGREE could lead to good adversarial robustness or not. 


[1] Tramer, Florian, et al. "On adaptive attacks to adversarial example defenses." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33 (2020): 1633-1645. 

[2] Bryniarski, Oliver, et al. "Evading Adversarial Example Detection Defenses with Orthogonal Projected Gradient Descent." International Conference on Learning Representations. 2021.

[3] Lee, Kimin, et al. "A simple unified framework for detecting out-of-distribution samples and adversarial attacks." Advances in neural information processing systems 31 (2018).

[4] Raghuram, Jayaram, et al. "A general framework for detecting anomalous inputs to DNN classifiers." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2021.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The writing is clear in general. The theoretical analysis seems novel. However, the experiments for evaluating the proposed defense method are limited.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes a new defense method called AGREE. However, the experimental evaluation of AGREE is limited and the results cannot demonstrate the effectiveness of AGREE under strong adaptive attacks. Thus, I recommend rejection.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper considers the detection of adversarial samples on the scenarios of simultaneous attacks, i.e., the quality of the detector should be generalized to different attacks exposed, instead of a specific one. To this end, authors propose a method by integrating multiple (pre-given/trained/pre-trained) detectors at hands , namely AGREE, which is built upon a surrogate loss by formalizing the simultaneous attacks as a minimax problem and using the average worst-cases regret. Empirical evaluations are conducted to verify the effectiveness of the method against simultaneous attacks. 

The main contributions, from the reviewer’s perspective (the reviewer has experiences on designing black-box adversarial attacks and victim-model-based defenses, though not exactly in the branch of adversarial detection), rely on the design of aggregating several detectors, i.e., AGREE, and its straightforward statistical explanations, i.e., the formalization of a minimax problem and an empirical solution corresponding to the derived upper bound.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The considered scenario, i.e., simultaneous attacks, is practically meaningful, as it is closely related to the real-world settings for more generalized adversarial detections without seeing all attack types, but lacks rich investigations in the existing literature.
2. Though the statistical explanations given in Sec. 3.1-3.2 is rather straightforward, it tries to formalize a solid objective for the simultaneous attacks being the interest of concern in this paper.
3. In the given settings (though not extensive enough), the performance improvemennt by of the basic idea behind AGREE looks quite promising, i.e., substantial improvements w.r.t. AUROC and FPR. For the used attacks themselves, it looks quite extensive enough for both white- and black-box settings with different perturbation  bounds.

Weakness

Majors:
1. Definition 1 gives the formal introduction of the proposed method, i.e., AGREE. Though thee paragraph ‘From theory to our practical detector’ briefly explains the connections between (10) and (11). More details could still be expected, as it is the central methodology of formulating the detection result in this paper. 

For instance, what’s the role of $\gamma$, or the set-up w.r.t. numerical evaluations; what does the $h_{\theta}$ refer to and represent from a technical aspect, compared to the single-model detector; what are the relations  between $h_{\theta}(x_0)$ and $u_0$? 

2. The resulting AGREE method is straightforward empirically and theoretically based on the given statistical perspective, thus the reviewer sees that the paper should give solid and more extensive numerical evidence to verify the soundness together with in-depth analysis. However, current experiments look a bit insufficient. Accordingly, some concerns are raised as follows.

2.1)  For the pre-trained classifiers, only ResNet-18 is used and it also seems that the adversarial training is not conducted.
 
2.1.1 - if the adversarial training is conducted, stronger adversarial samples shall be expected, which is helpful in giving more solid verifications on the ability of the proposed method. Why or why not use this set-up?

2.1.2 - similarly, I would like to know how authors think about only choosing a single architecture, e.g., what if more sophisticated network architectures are used besides the Restnet-18, how much can the proposed method improve, or can be expected?

2.2) Aside of sec3.1-3.2, the resulting (10) and (11) are actually in strong relation to the idea of ensemble method. For instance in [1], the detection is based on the weighting of different models, i.e., the weighting scheme is simply taken as the average. 

2.2.1 - it could help better understand the proposed method and its contributions, if authors make some clarifications on the relations to (at least) the  ensemble method, or other similar ideas, such as bagging or boosting. 

2.2.2 - in the appendix, it shows that the optimization toolbox is used for the resulting concave function, and the initial point is given as  the average weighting, which is similar to [1] and already shows satisfactory results in [1]. Can authors report the performance at the initial point [0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25] and see how much  the optimization on $w_k$  can improve?

2.2.3 - though the optimization of $w_k$ depends on the chosen algorithm and its settings, brief analyses on the computation complexity or at least some remarks  are  essential in presenting the proposed method. I would like to suggest the authors include some content into the main body of the paper.

2.3) the efficiency is of concern as multiple detectors should be used and the sample-wise optimization at evaluation takes much more extra time, as shown in sec B.1.1. 

2.4) the  choice of the solo compared method, i.e., NSS, is too dependent on the reliability of the results on paper [2].

2.5) the whole paper only consider 4 detectors ($|\mathcal K|$ is always 4) trained under the same settings (trained with clean and pgd-adv samples with different loss functions), which is not extensive enough in giving in-depth investigations, as it can actually be the ablation study and also plays a crucial role on the computational cost of the proposed method. 

Weakness

Minors:
1. In the fifth line of the 1st paragraph in section 1, the ‘category’ of robustness is not precise enough, as other mentioned works in parallel are all about robustness.
2. In the 2nd paragraph of section 4, it states that ‘…each of them is trained to detect only specific kind of attack’ while in the paragraph of Detectors in section 4.1, it states that each detector is trained with pdg of the same bound but with different loss function. Such two states are not strictly consistent enough, as what’s the exact ‘definition of the diversified detectors’, the attacking algorithm in training or the loss?
3. Have the authors considered that whether aggregating weaker detectors  is better or aggregating strong enough detectors  is better? E.g., boosting and bagging normally consider relatively weaker submodels for better performances.
4. Is it possible to detect some ‘properties’ of the $w_k$ for clean and adversarial samples, for instance, their distributions w.r.t. these four detectors; the individual  effect of these four detectors, the learned features (or decision boundary characteristics)on individual detectors or the final detector, etc.
5. In the appendix, the autoattack is tested with some modifications. It looks that it’s still possible to compare with NSS. Why not conduct so?
6. TinyImagnet should be feasible without significantly complicating the experiments. 


 
[1] Steinberg, Daniel, and Paul Munro. "Measuring the Contribution of Multiple Model Representations in Detecting Adversarial Instances." AAAI-22 AdvML Workshop LongPaper

[2]Granese, Federica, et al. "MEAD: A Multi-Armed Approach for Evaluation of Adversarial Examples Detectors." arXiv preprint arXiv:2206.15415 (2022).
content.summary_of_the_review:
The tackled problem is of interest to the community, particularly regarding real-world settings, and the proposed method seems effective. However, more in-depth and rigorous discussions and empirical evaluations can be expected to verify this simple and yet useful method.
The current recommendation is based on the above mentioned concerns, most related to the lack of discussions on the details of the proposed methodology  and empirical soundness. The reviewer's evaluation could be reconsidered, if authors could well address those concerns.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focuses on adversarial examples detection, where the adversarial examples could be generated by one of many different kinds of adversarial attacks. This setting makes any detectors that are specifically trained for a certain kind of adversarial attack fail. To solve this problem, they propose an aggregating strategy to learn weights on the output of some known specialized detectors. They use the weighted average probability distribution to detect adversarial examples. Their method obtains better results than SOTA.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The method is simple yet effective. They simply need to learn weights on any given networks that output probability distribution.
2. They give a thorough evaluation of their methods. They obtain better results in some cases. They also admit to some failures.

Weaknesses (including some of my questions):
1. Why do we need a min-max formulation? I know 'min', but I think 'max' might not be the only choice for aggregation loss.
2. Suppose we adopt a min-max formulation; why is it more challenging to optimize than your final max-min problem?
3. AGREE is only designed for aggregating some known detectors. This setting is more restricted and easier compared with training a detector from scratch, and to some degree, makes the results less contributed.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: They introduce the problem and setting clearly. They describe the details of their methods, and I think it should not be hard to reproduce if all the parameters are further given.
content.summary_of_the_review: This simple yet effective method obtains some progress in detecting adversarial examples. Due to the weaknesses I propose above, I would like to give a weak rejection currently.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.

content.title: Response to Reviewe nZhm
content.comment:
*We thank the reviewer for the positive feedback and questions that helped us clarify and improve our paper.*

**Weaknesses**

1. Although the ‘max’ in the minmax formulation is not the only possible aggregation strategy as underlined by the reviewer, this is the only aggregation strategy that accounts for the worst case scenario, i.e. when we consider the strongest attacker which maximizes the negative log-likelihood of the predictions over the pool of available detectors.

2. The equality of the minmax and maxmin problem in equation 9 means that the solution to our problem is a saddle point and can be obtained according to the classical min-max theorem (c.f. von Neumann 1928). For further details concerning this formulation, we reference the Supplementary material, Sec. A.1, Proof of Eq. (9).

3. According to Section 3, AGREE aggregates a set of available soft-detectors models, which have possibly been trained to detect attacks according to each strategy $k\in\mathcal{K}$. Indeed, $\mathcal{K}$ does not necessarily need to be the set of all possible attacks (which may not be a finite number). In the experiments, we evaluate AGREE on a much larger amount of attacks than those available to the individual detectors at training time. In principle, it could be possible to collect an arbitrarily large and diverse amount of samples (both natural and adversarial) and aim to train a single detection model. If we consider that each different attack creates a different shift in the natural sample's distribution, we may think of a model that generalizes to many domains over the same label space. One may argue that such a model would be convoluted and hard to train, but let us suppose, for the sake of argument, that we can find an abstract representation of the attacks provided at training time which makes it possible to have such a model. We argue that, even in this case, our proposed solution has an important advantage. Indeed, supposing that we want to adapt the general single model to a new attack, i.e. to a new domain, this would require a new training procedure which may be time-consuming or a fine-tuning which may be demanding in terms of parameters optimization. Our solution would simply work by aggregating a new detector and computing its weight w.r.t. the other detectors and the task at hand.

*We hope we have addressed most of your comments satisfactorily and kindly request you to revise your score.*

content.title: about 'max' in the min-max formulation
content.comment:
I still don't get why we need to care about the worst-case scenario most here. Suppose we have K possible different attacks. The question is quite simple: given K distributions on a finite set, we want to find a distribution that is close to them. Why do we need to consider the worst-case scenario? What if this leads to some kind of average, which means all K losses are nearly equally big? Why don't we use 'sum' to control all of these? 

From another point of view, one of these K distributions corresponds to the real attack. Ideally, the learned distribution should be identical to this one. We actually don't care how far the learned distribution is to a distribution corresponding to a wrong attack. So doesn't this mean a min-min formulation or a min-sum(bottom p), e.g., p=3  is better?

content.comment:
$\widehat{Z}$ represents the detector’s inference random variable, and $q_{\widehat{Z}|\mathbf{u_{0}}}$ represents the probability of being either an adversarial or a natural example according to the distribution output by the detector. This is reported in Sec. 3.1, c.f. definition of $\mathcal{Q}$ and the following paragraph. We will update the paper to make this even more clear, however we think that the reviewer may have missed this part since s/he admits that math/other details were not carefully checked.

The reviewer says that several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported, however no detailed concerns are reported. Therefore, we would like to raise a concern about the integrity of this review since, in our honest opinion, the comments are rather general and do not address any specific technical concerns about the paper. In addition, a similar review at this link (https://openreview.net/forum?id=mCmerkTCG2S&noteId=lsu_sDt1UIF) has been flagged and eventually erased.
